keyPoints.text: Permission modes set default tool behavior: default prompts, acceptEdits auto-approves edits, plan forbids edits, bypassPermissions approves all.
A canUseTool callback provides runtime human-in-the-loop approval for calls no rule resolves.
Deny rules and PreToolUse hooks block a call deterministically, even under bypassPermissions.
Hooks give deterministic guarantees; prompt instructions alone are only probabilistic.
The Agent SDK provides Claude Code's agent loop, built-in tools, and context management as a Python and TypeScript library.
You call query() with a prompt and options, and the SDK runs the loop and executes tools for you.
With the base Client SDK you implement the tool loop yourself; the Agent SDK handles it autonomously.
Sessions let you resume a run with full context or fork it to explore a different approach.
The agentic loop is: act, observe ground truth from the environment, decide, and repeat.
stop_reason "tool_use" means run the tool and return a tool_result in a new user message to continue.
stop_reason "end_turn" means Claude finished naturally, so the loop ends.
Add stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations to keep control.
AI Fluency is interacting with AI in ways that are effective, efficient, ethical, and safe.
Delegation is thoughtfully deciding what to do with AI versus doing it yourself.
Description is communicating clearly with the AI; Discernment is critically evaluating its outputs and behavior.
Diligence is interacting with AI responsibly, including verifying results before relying on them.
The augmented LLM is the basic building block of agentic systems.
Its three augmentations are retrieval, tools, and memory.
The model actively uses them: generating its own search queries, selecting tools, and choosing what to retain.
Tailor the augmentations to your use case and give each a clean, well-documented interface.
Concept cards open with an analogy, then an explain-back asks you to teach the idea so gaps surface early.
Questions you miss go into a spaced-repetition review deck that resurfaces them over time.
Mock exams mirror the real 60-question, 120-minute, weighted format.
The app tags every question by domain weight so practice matches where the exam spends points.
The app is study prep only; Anthropic administers the paid certification and no app can guarantee a pass.
The exam is 60 questions answered in 120 minutes.
The five domains are weighted: Agentic Architecture 27 percent, Claude Code 20 percent, Prompt Engineering 20 percent, Tool Design and MCP 18 percent, and Context Management 15 percent.
You pass with a scaled score of 720, and the report shows percent correct per domain, not five separate cut lines.
The exam covers Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, the Claude API, and MCP.
Prep effort should track domain weight, so the 27 percent domain deserves the most study time.
Items are scenario-first: they ask which design fits a situation, not what a term means.
Each sitting draws 4 scenario clusters from a published bank of 6.
The six scenarios span a customer-support agent, Claude Code code generation, a multi-agent research system, developer productivity tools, Claude Code CI/CD, and structured data extraction.
Items are multiple choice or multiple response, and each item tells you how many answers to select.
Distractors are plausible but flawed architectures, so you eliminate by tradeoff, not by keyword.
Chain-of-thought asks Claude to reason step by step before answering, improving accuracy on complex multi-step tasks.
The tradeoff is longer output and higher latency, so reserve extended reasoning for problems that need multi-step reasoning.
Claude must output its reasoning to benefit; use <thinking> and <answer> tags to separate reasoning from the final answer.
Current models use adaptive thinking with the effort setting to control depth; manual budget_tokens is deprecated.
Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a fixed sequence where each LLM call processes the previous call's output.
You can add programmatic gate checks between chained steps to catch errors before they propagate.
Routing classifies an input and sends it to a specialized follow-up task, enabling separation of concerns.
Use chaining when subtasks are fixed and sequential; use routing when distinct categories are handled better separately and classification is accurate.
Hooks run at fixed lifecycle events such as PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, and Stop.
Exit code 0 is success; exit code 2 is a blocking error whose stderr is fed back to Claude; any other non-zero code is a non-blocking error.
A PreToolUse hook that exits 2 blocks the tool call before it runs.
Hooks enforce deterministically regardless of what Claude decides, so use one when an action must be blocked every time, unlike a probabilistic CLAUDE.md instruction.
CLAUDE.md can live at managed-policy, user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), and project (./CLAUDE.md) scopes, loaded broadest first down to your working directory.
User CLAUDE.md is personal and not shared through version control; project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared with the team.
Discovered CLAUDE.md files are concatenated into context, not overridden, so an instruction closer to your working directory is read last but does not erase the others.
The @path syntax imports other files (recursively, up to four hops); to verify which memory files loaded, the exam guide names /memory and current Claude Code docs say /context.
Clear, explicit, specific instructions produce better results than vague prompts; state the exact output format and constraints.
Golden rule of clear prompting: if a colleague with minimal context would be confused by your prompt, Claude will be too.
Give instructions as sequential numbered steps when order matters, and add context or motivation so Claude can generalize.
Set a role in the system prompt to focus Claude behavior and tone for your use case.
Server-side compaction summarizes older conversation near the window limit into a compaction block and drops prior blocks so the conversation can continue.
Claude Code auto-compacts long sessions on the same principle of replacing older content with a concise summary.
The memory tool stores facts in files outside the context window and reads them back on demand across sessions.
For long-running agents, pair them: compaction keeps active context small while memory preserves facts that must survive summarization.
Context editing clears older tool results once context passes a configured trigger, replacing each with a placeholder so the model knows it was removed.
The trigger defaults to 100,000 input tokens and keep defaults to the 3 most recent tool uses.
exclude_tools protects specific tools from clearing, and clear_tool_inputs also removes the original tool calls.
Clearing invalidates the cached prefix, so use clear_at_least to clear enough tokens to make breaking the cache worthwhile.
Context engineering is curating the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of the desired outcome.
Every token spends a limited attention budget, so more context is not automatically better.
Trim verbose tool results to the relevant fields and prefer just-in-time retrieval over loading everything up front.
For long horizons, use compaction, structured note-taking, and sub-agents that return condensed summaries.
The context window is all the tokens a model can reference, including its own output, and it is finite working memory.
As the token count grows, recall and accuracy degrade; this documented effect is called context rot, and it is a gradient, not a hard cliff.
Everything counts toward the window: system prompt, every message, tool results, tool definitions, and the generated output including thinking.
Because recall degrades with size, curating what is in context matters as much as how large the window is.
stop_reason reports why generation stopped: end_turn is done, tool_use means run a tool, and max_tokens means the output was truncated.
pause_turn means a server-tool loop paused, so send the assistant content back to continue; refusal means read stop_details.
Transient HTTP errors (429 rate_limit_error, 500 api_error, 529 overloaded_error) are retryable with exponential backoff, honoring the retry-after header.
Client errors like 400, 401, 403, and 404 are terminal: fix the request rather than retrying it.
Agents should pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit a blocker they cannot resolve, not run autonomously without limits.
When a request is ambiguous, such as multiple matching records, ask for a disambiguating detail instead of guessing one.
Propagate structured error context (what failed, what was attempted, partial results) so a coordinator can adapt and resume rather than restart.
Silently swallowing a failure and terminating the whole workflow on one failure are both anti-patterns; keep partial results and preserve claim-to-source citations in synthesis.
Verification is part of the agent loop; rules-based feedback like linters and tests is the strongest signal.
Good rules-based feedback states which rule failed and why, so the agent can self-correct.
LLM-as-judge is possible but generally less robust and adds latency, so use it only when the gain justifies the cost.
For long runs, resume from where the agent was rather than restarting, and a fresh session with a structured summary can beat stale results.
Force machine-readable output with Structured Outputs (JSON schema) or strict tool use (schema-validated tool inputs).
Prefilling the last assistant turn to force a format is unsupported on current models and returns a 400 error; migrate to structured outputs or tools.
A validation-and-retry loop that feeds the specific validation error back fixes format and structural errors.
Retries do not recover information the source never contained, so separate format errors from missing data.
Few-shot (multishot) prompting steers output format, tone, and structure more reliably than instructions alone.
Include 3 to 5 examples for best results.
Make examples relevant, diverse (covering edge cases), and structured with <example> tags inside <examples>.
Diverse examples stop Claude from picking up unintended patterns, and tags separate examples from instructions.
Claude Code can create git commits and pull requests on request, and git worktrees run parallel sessions as separate checkouts each on its own branch.
Committing a project CLAUDE.md and project settings (.claude/settings.json) standardizes the whole team through version control.
Personal files like CLAUDE.local.md and .claude/settings.local.json stay private and gitignored, so they do not standardize the team.
Documenting testing standards, conventions, and fixtures in CLAUDE.md improves the quality of the tests Claude generates, which you then iterate by running and fixing.
Explicitly allowing Claude to say it does not know or lacks enough information sharply reduces false information.
Ground answers by asking for direct quotes first and restricting Claude to the provided documents.
Make output auditable: have Claude cite a supporting quote for each claim and retract claims it cannot support.
In extraction, optional or nullable fields let Claude leave data blank instead of fabricating when the source lacks it.
claude -p (--print) runs non-interactively, reading stdin and printing a result, so it fits scripts, pre-commit hooks, and CI.
--output-format json returns a structured payload, and --json-schema constrains the output into a structured_output field for machine parsing.
A separate, independent review instance catches more than self-review, because the generating session retains its own reasoning context.
The GitHub Actions integration responds to @claude mentions and reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from repository secrets, with CLAUDE.md providing project context.
A lead agent analyzes the request, decomposes it, delegates to subagents, and synthesizes their results.
Each subagent needs an explicit objective, output format, tool and source guidance, and clear task boundaries.
Vague delegation causes duplicated work and coverage gaps.
Inter-subagent communication routes through the coordinator, not directly between workers.
For large inputs (20k or more tokens), place long documents at the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions, and examples.
Putting the query at the end can improve response quality, especially for complex multi-document inputs.
Structure multiple documents with <document>, <document_content>, and <source> tags for clarity.
Ask Claude to extract relevant quotes first, then answer based on those quotes, to cut through document noise.
Sampling let a server request an LLM completion from the client (sampling/createMessage); it is deprecated as of protocol 2026-07-28, and new servers should call LLM provider APIs directly.
Elicitation lets a server request additional information or confirmation from the user (elicitation/create).
Roots let the client tell the server which filesystem directories are in scope, coordinating boundaries without enforcing security; they are deprecated as of protocol 2026-07-28.
Notifications, such as tools/list_changed, inform the client of changes and expect no response.
MCP has three participants: a host (the AI application), clients, and servers.
The host creates one client per server, and each client keeps a dedicated one-to-one connection.
The server is the program that provides context and capabilities to a client.
The data layer uses JSON-RPC 2.0 for messages; the transport layer carries them.
Local scope is the default, private to you in the current project, stored in ~/.claude.json.
Project scope is shared with the team via a .mcp.json file checked into version control.
User scope makes a server available across all your projects.
When a name exists at multiple scopes, precedence is local, then project, then user; use ${VAR} expansion to keep secrets out of version control.
Tools are model-controlled functions the model invokes to take actions, via tools/list and tools/call.
Resources are application-controlled, read-only data sources that provide context, each identified by a URI.
Prompts are user-controlled reusable templates that require explicit invocation, via prompts/list and prompts/get.
Control differs by primitive: tools are model-controlled, resources application-controlled, and prompts user-controlled.
The stdio transport uses standard input/output for local, same-machine processes with no network overhead.
The Streamable HTTP transport uses HTTP POST with optional Server-Sent Events and enables remote servers.
HTTP transport supports standard auth like bearer tokens and API keys; MCP recommends OAuth to obtain tokens.
Local stdio servers typically serve one client; remote HTTP servers can serve many clients.

When an instruction is ignored, first verify which CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and rules files actually loaded; the exam guide names /memory for this, and current Claude Code docs say /context lists loaded files while /memory lists and opens them.
CLAUDE.md files are written by you and load in full every session; auto memory is written by Claude and its MEMORY.md index loads within a size cap (first 200 lines or 25KB).
Instructions given only in chat can be lost, so lasting instructions belong in CLAUDE.md rather than a one-off message.
A project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk and survives /compact, while nested subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are not re-injected automatically.
The Message Batches API processes large volumes of requests asynchronously at 50% lower cost.
Most batches finish within an hour but may take up to 24 hours; requests not completed by then expire.
Each request has a custom_id to correlate results, which can come back in any order.
Use batches for high-volume, latency-tolerant work like evaluations or overnight reports, not blocking time-sensitive requests.
Agents use about 4x the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15x, so cost multiplies fast.
Token usage explains most of the performance variance, so multi-agent only pays off when the task value justifies the cost.
Multi-agent excels at high-value, breadth-first tasks that parallelize and exceed a single context window.
It is a poor fit when agents must share the same context or have many dependencies between them.
Orchestrator-workers uses a central LLM that dynamically breaks down a task, delegates to workers, and synthesizes results.
The key difference from parallelization is that subtasks are determined by the orchestrator at runtime, not predefined.
Evaluator-optimizer has one LLM generate a response while another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop.
Use evaluator-optimizer when you have clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement provides measurable value.
Spawn subagents in parallel when their subtasks are independent, which speeds up breadth-first work.
Run subagents sequentially when a later subtask depends on an earlier subtask's result.
Parallel spawning means issuing multiple subagent calls in a single response.
On failure, resume from where the agent was rather than restarting, and let the agent adapt when a tool is failing.
Parallelization runs LLM calls simultaneously, in two variations: sectioning and voting.
Sectioning breaks a task into independent subtasks run in parallel.
Voting runs the same task multiple times to get diverse outputs you then aggregate.
Use it when subtasks parallelize for speed, or when multiple perspectives or attempts raise confidence.
Rules live as topic files under .claude/rules/ and are discovered recursively.
A `paths:` glob frontmatter scopes a rule so it loads only when Claude works with matching files, saving context.
A rule with no `paths` field loads unconditionally, at the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md.
Glob-scoped rules beat a directory CLAUDE.md when a convention spans directories, such as **/*.test.ts.
default (Manual) prompts on first use of each tool; acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands in the working directory.
plan mode reads only and makes no edits to source files; bypassPermissions skips permission prompts and is for isolated containers or VMs only.
Permission rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins.
A deny rule beats a matching allow rule regardless of specificity, and explicit ask rules still prompt even under bypassPermissions.
Plan mode has Claude research and propose changes without editing source; no edits happen until you approve the plan.
Enter plan mode with Shift+Tab or --permission-mode plan; approving a plan exits plan mode and starts editing.
Use plan mode for large-scale, architectural, multi-approach, or multi-file work and unfamiliar code; use direct execution for well-scoped, clear changes.
The built-in Plan subagent researches in its own context window and skips CLAUDE.md and git status to keep exploration cheap.
Prompt caching reuses a stable prefix; you mark up to 4 cache breakpoints with cache_control.
The default cache lifetime is 5 minutes, with an optional 1-hour TTL at higher write cost.
Cache writes cost more than base input (1.25x for 5 minutes) while cache reads cost only 0.1x.
The cached prefix follows tools then system then messages; changing content at or before a breakpoint invalidates that level and everything after it.
Put stable content first and volatile content last so a small change does not invalidate the whole prefix, and remember cached tokens still occupy the window.
Rate limits apply per model as RPM, ITPM (input tokens per minute), and OTPM (output tokens per minute).
The token bucket algorithm continuously replenishes capacity rather than resetting at fixed intervals, so short bursts can still trip a limit.
On most models only uncached input counts toward ITPM, so prompt caching raises effective throughput, and max_tokens does not factor into OTPM.
Streaming sends the response incrementally over server-sent events, and an error can still arrive mid-stream after the initial 200 response.
Ordinary settings resolve by precedence: managed, then command-line args, then local, then project, then user.
Managed (enterprise) settings are highest and cannot be overridden by any other level, including command-line arguments.
Permission rules do not override across scopes; allow, ask, and deny rules merge from every scope.
A deny rule at any scope beats an allow at another, so if a tool is denied anywhere no other level can allow it.
A skill is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter and instructions, invoked by /skill-name or loaded by Claude when relevant.
A skill body loads only when used (progressive disclosure), while CLAUDE.md always loads, so procedures go in skills and standing facts in CLAUDE.md.
Skills live at project, personal (~/.claude/skills/), or enterprise scope, and on a name clash enterprise overrides personal overrides project.
Frontmatter tunes behavior: allowed-tools pre-approves tools while active, disable-model-invocation makes a skill user-only, and argument-hint guides expected input.
Structured Outputs use constrained decoding to guarantee responses conform to your JSON schema, eliminating parse errors and missing required fields.
Enable JSON output with output_config.format set to type json_schema plus your schema.
The schema is guaranteed but the values are not: Claude can still return semantically wrong data that still validates.
On a refusal (stop_reason "refusal") or truncation (stop_reason "max_tokens"), the output may not match the schema; retry with higher max_tokens.
A subagent runs in its own isolated context window with a custom system prompt and specific tool access.
The main agent delegates a focused task and the subagent returns only its results, keeping the main context clean.
Subagents preserve context, enforce tool constraints, and specialize behavior with focused prompts.
Routing a subagent to a faster, cheaper model can control cost.

A subagent is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter (name, description, tools, model) in .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/, running in its own context window with a custom prompt and restricted tools.
An MCP server connects Claude Code to external tools and data, rather than being an isolated worker like a subagent.
MCP scopes are local (default, private), project (.mcp.json, shared and committed to version control), and user (all your projects), with local taking precedence over project over user.
Environment-variable expansion like ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in .mcp.json keeps secrets out of version control while sharing the config.
Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and usually multidimensional (accuracy, latency, cost).
Define success criteria before building so you can measure progress against them.
Build empirical evals from many test cases that mirror real usage and edge cases.
Prefer automated grading (exact match, code-based, LLM-based) at high volume over a few hand-graded cases.
The count_tokens endpoint returns the input_tokens a request would use before you send it.
It accepts the same inputs as Messages (system, messages, tools, images, PDFs) and returns an estimate, not a billed message.
It is free to use but has its own requests-per-minute limits, separate from message creation.
Use it to budget against rate limits and cost, route between models, and fit prompts to a target length.
tool_choice "auto" lets Claude decide whether to call a tool and is the default when tools are provided.
tool_choice "any" forces Claude to call one of the provided tools but does not force a particular one.
tool_choice {"type":"tool","name":...} forces one specific named tool, and "none" prevents tool use.
disable_parallel_tool_use: true limits Claude to at most one tool call per turn.
A tool definition has three parts: a name, a description, and an input_schema.
The description is by far the most important factor in tool performance, because Claude selects tools from their descriptions.
A good description states what the tool does, when to use it and when not, and what each parameter means.
The input_schema is a JSON Schema object that defines the tool's expected parameters.
Return a tool execution error in the tool_result content with is_error set to true.
Write instructive error messages that say what went wrong and what to try next, not a generic "failed".
Distinguish retryable errors (like a rate limit) from terminal ones so the agent can retry or stop.
strict: true constrains tool inputs to match the JSON schema, eliminating missing-parameter and type errors.
For client tools, Claude returns stop_reason "tool_use" and one or more tool_use blocks, and your code executes the tool.
You return each result in a tool_result block in a new user message, matched to its call by tool_use_id.
You loop while stop_reason is "tool_use" and exit on any other stop reason, such as "end_turn".
Client tools run in your application; server tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure and need no tool_result from you.
Find the simplest solution first and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
The simplest solution is sometimes not an agentic system at all.
Agentic systems trade latency and cost for better task performance, so weigh that tradeoff.
Use agents for open-ended problems where you cannot predict the steps or hardcode the path.
A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths.
An agent lets the model dynamically direct its own process and tool use.
Choose a workflow for predictable, well-defined tasks; choose an agent when the steps cannot be predicted in advance.
Start with the simplest solution and add agentic complexity only when it earns its extra cost and latency.
Build fewer, more capable tools that consolidate related operations instead of wrapping every API endpoint.
Return high-signal, token-efficient results using pagination, filtering, and truncation with sensible defaults.
Prefer meaningful identifiers over opaque UUIDs to reduce hallucination.
Choose the right built-in tool: Grep searches file contents, Glob finds files by name, and Edit makes targeted string replacements.
XML tags let Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously; wrap each content type in its own descriptive tag.
Use consistent, descriptive tag names and nest tags when content has a natural hierarchy.
Prompt templates separate fixed instructions from variable inputs (double-bracket placeholders) so prompts stay consistent and testable.
Steer formatting by telling Claude what to do instead of what not to do, and by using XML tags as format indicators.
